source: FAO Regional Office for Asia and the Pacific, Swine Health Management, Volume 2: Guide to Prevent and Control Porcine Reproductive and Respiratory Syndrome (RAP Publication 2012/27, Bangkok, 2012)
text: In weaned and growing pigs, PRRS can cause loss of appetite, sluggish movement, labored or rapid breathing, blotchy red patches on the skin, a rough hair coat, and huddling together (which can be a sign of fever). The disease is most often seen in pigs 4 to 12 weeks old. Secondary bacterial infections commonly appear in pigs 12 to 16 weeks old, often causing lameness. Death rates in this age group can reach 12 to 15 percent. When PRRS first enters a herd that has never had it before, signs in growing pigs can be mild at first — reduced appetite and light coughing — and only become severe once other diseases like pneumonia are also present.
